Idea

The meter measures the light on your easel and turns it into a printing time: light × your paper's constant = seconds. Every tool is built on that one number. Once your paper is calibrated, any new reading becomes a time immediately.

How to use this manual

There are three ways in:

If you want to…Start at
Connect the dongle and make a first print1. Start here
Look up one control you can see on screen15. Reference → Index of controls
Fix a problem13. Messages and troubleshooting

The manual follows the product: first the dongle and the app shell, then the five tools, then Setup and the jobs that need several steps (paper calibration, files, firmware updates).

Words in this manual. A control is something you tap, drag or type into. A readout is a number or message the app shows you. Names printed in bold match the labels on screen. The dongle has no display: every screen in this manual is on the Android phone.

Tip

The HTML edition (open MANUAL.html in a browser) has a Darkroom button that switches to red-on-black. Use it on a phone or tablet beside the enlarger.

Note

The paper catalogue, the calibration, the filter brand and grade, the trims and the session settings live on the dongle. The app reads them on every connection. There is no bundled paper list in the app, and no file is loaded at launch. If the app says Connect the meter to list papers, the paper list is simply not available until the dongle answers.

1. Start here

1.1 What the dongle does

The SafelightIO dongle is a small USB-C light meter. One end plugs into the phone; the other end carries the light sensor. It measures the light on the easel and works out how long to expose the paper.

It is the same metering engine as the 7-inch SafelightIO, without the screen. The dongle has:

  • the TSL2591 light sensor and its dark/light calibration;
  • the RP2350 processor running the same exposure, contrast and split-grade arithmetic;
  • the paper catalogue, the filter brands and grades, and the paper constants;
  • the per-paper trims and burn records;
  • USB-C, which carries both power and the text protocol.

It has no display, no battery and no BOOTSEL button. The phone supplies the screen, the keyboard and the touch input. The dongle supplies the measurement. A computer is not needed to use the meter; a computer is needed only for a firmware update.

1.2 The one thing that makes it accurate

A light reading on its own is not a printing time. The meter needs to know what your paper and developer do with that light. The paper calibration is the bridge: one test strip gives the dongle two numbers, and it multiplies them to get the paper's constant.

After that, the answer is just multiplication. The dongle does it; the app shows it. The phone never does the metering arithmetic and never needs a network connection.

1.3 What you need

  • An Android phone with USB-C and USB host (OTG) support.
  • The SafelightIO Android app installed on the phone.
  • The SafelightIO dongle.
  • A USB-C cable or a USB-C OTG adapter that passes data, not just power.
  • Your paper, your filter brand and a test strip for the paper calibration.
  • Optional: a computer and a USB cable for firmware updates.

Important

Use a data cable. A charge-only cable can power the dongle but the app will never see it. If the phone offers a USB permission dialog, choose Allow.

1.4 Your first session

StepWhat you doWhere
1Plug the dongle into the phoneUSB-C
2Allow the USB permissionAndroid dialog
3Choose the filter brand and the paperPaper & filter sheet
4Calibrate the sensor: dark, then enlarger lightSetup → Sensor → Sensor Calibration
5Calibrate the paper with one test stripSetup → Calibration or Tools & data → Estimate Calibration
6Measure the easel and printExposure

Steps 4 and 5 are one-time jobs per device and paper. Step 3 is repeated when you change paper. Step 6 is the everyday job.

Step 1 — Connect the dongle

Plug the dongle into the phone. Android asks whether to allow the app to access the USB device; choose Allow. The app's top bar moves from No meter to Linking, then to Ready · fw 0.11 (your firmware version may be newer).

If the app says No meter and no dialog appears, unplug the dongle, check that the cable is a data cable, and plug it in again. On some phones the USB mode must be set to File transfer / MTP or USB controlled by this device; the app will show the permission dialog either way.

Step 2 — Choose the paper and filter

Tap the selection bar under the top bar: it reads No paper | No filter until something is chosen. The Paper & filter sheet opens.

  1. Choose the Filter brand in the rail at the top.
  2. Open the paper brand's row and choose the paper.

The sheet does not ask for a filter grade. The grade is chosen on Exposure because it belongs to the exposure, not to the paper selection.

With no meter connected, the sheet says Connect the meter to list papers. That is not an error: the list is on the dongle.

Step 3 — Choose the zone

On Exposure, the zone rail is already at Zone V, the usual starting point. Swipe the rail or tap a neighbouring zone to change it. The selected value settles in the centre; the app shows zone V in the line under the answer.

Step 4 — Calibrate the sensor

Open Setup → Sensor → Sensor Calibration. Do Calibrate Dark with the sensor covered, then Calibrate Enlarger Light with the enlarger on and the sensor in the light. This is the sensor's zero and its reference; it is one of the two calibrations that make the lux numbers trustworthy.

Step 5 — Calibrate the paper

Open Setup → Calibration and enter the Known lux and Known time from a test strip, or use Setup → Tools & data → Estimate Calibration to estimate the pair. Follow the steps in chapter 10. The dongle stores the paper's constant; the app reads it back on every connection.

Step 6 — Measure and print

Return to Exposure. Put the sensor on the easel, tap Measure, and read the time. Set the enlarger to that time, with the suggested filter grade, and make the print.

Tip

The meter predicts; the strip confirms. If the print is consistently too light or too dark, check the paper calibration before changing the meter's answer.

1.5 The five tools at a glance

ToolWhat it answersWhat you do
ExposureOne printing time for the easel readingChoose a zone, Measure, use the time and grade
ContrastA time and a suggested grade from a highlight and a shadowMeasure the dim spot, then the bright spot
SplitA soft time and a hard time for a two-filter printMeasure the same two spots; use the pair
ProofA grid of the print, and optionally the enlarger's evennessScan the grid, tap cells, read the verdict
SetupDevice, calibration, sensor, files and helpOpen the page you need

Every tool starts with its answer at the top of the screen. If there is no answer yet, the answer area says so and tells you which measurement is missing.

2. The app at a glance

2.1 The shell

Every tool uses the same shell:

  • Top bar: the SafelightIO wordmark on the left and the meter state on the right. The state is No meter, Linking, Ready · fw … or a short error. Tap it to open Setup → Meter.
  • Selection bar: the paper on the left and the filter brand on the right. Tap it to open Paper & filter. This is the only place the paper and brand are chosen.
  • Content: the current tool. The answer, the controls and the reference cards live here.
  • Bottom navigation: Exposure, Contrast, Split, Proof and Setup. The active item has a tonal capsule.

The app hides the Android status bar while it is in front. The page background runs to the top of the screen, so there is no black strip above the interface.

2.2 The Paper & filter sheet

The sheet has two sections:

  1. Filter brand at the top, as a horizontal rail. Choose the brand before the paper: the brand determines which paper rows and which grades are valid.
  2. Paper below it, one collapsible row per manufacturer. The row shows the paper count; open it and choose the paper. The paper in force is marked In use.

There is no filter grade in this sheet. The grade is a property of the exposure and is chosen in Filter Grade Transform on the Exposure screen. This is deliberate: a grade chosen while picking paper would be a second, competing authority for the same number.

Note

The bar shows the paper and the filter brand — for example Ilford MGT Cooltone | Ilford. It never shows a grade. If no brand is in force it reads No filter.

2.3 Setup is the index

Tap Setup in the bottom navigation. The index has three groups:

GroupPages
DeviceMeter, Paper & filter
CalibrationCalibration, Sensor
WorkTools & data, Help & messages, About

The index is not a settings dump. Each row opens a page with one job. The Meter page reports the connection and firmware; Paper & filter opens the same sheet as the selection bar; Calibration is the paper's two numbers; Sensor is gain, integration time, averaging and the Sensor Calibration card.

2.4 Connecting, reconnecting and the USB permission

The dongle is a USB device. The first connection raises Android's permission dialog. After that, the app can reopen the port when the dongle is plugged in again.

Top bar saysMeaning
No meterNo dongle is attached, or Android has not granted access
LinkingThe app is opening the port and waiting for HELLO
Ready · fw 0.11The dongle answered; the app is reading its catalogue and settings
A short errorThe port opened but the dongle did not answer, or the firmware refused

If the state stays on No meter, open Setup → Meter and use Reconnect. If that fails, unplug and replug the dongle. If the phone has a USB mode switch, set it to allow the connected device.

Important

Close any other app that is holding the USB port. Android gives the port to one app at a time. The SafelightIO app will show No meter if another app owns it.

2.5 What the dongle keeps and what the phone keeps

The dongle keeps the things that belong to the meter:

  • the paper and filter catalogue;
  • the paper calibrations;
  • the filter brand and grade in force;
  • the sensor gain, integration time and averaging;
  • the per-paper trims and burn;
  • the trims and burn the app writes back while you work.

The phone keeps:

  • the app itself;
  • the saved settings and session files in the Data Manager;
  • the screen and the reader's current view.

The app is not a copy of the dongle. If you connect the same dongle to another phone, the catalogue and calibrations are still there; the files on the old phone are not.

3. Exposure

3.1 The screen

From top to bottom:

  1. No reading (or the time) in the answer well. Under it, one line of conditions: burn, grade, zone.
  2. A zone rule with a dot at the selected zone. It is a picture of where the reading sits on the 0–X scale, not a second control.
  3. Measure — the one action. It is disabled when the dongle is not ready.
  4. Exposure Calculator — the zone rail, the Lux reading and the Calibration constant.
  5. Filter Grade Transform — the grade rail, or the reason there is no grade.
  6. Dodge & Burn — the burn slider.

The answer well keeps the same height even when a long time shrinks to fit, or when the conditions line wraps to two lines. The controls below do not jump.

3.2 Every control and readout

Zone rail

Zone of measurement is a horizontal snap rail from 0 to X. The selected zone sits in the centre; the neighbouring zones peek in at the edges. Swipe the rail or tap a neighbour. The rail snaps to a whole zone, the dongle saves it, and the app recomputes the answer from the stored reading.

Lux reading

The illuminance the dongle measured, in lux. It is the number the time is computed from. When no reading has been taken, it shows —.

Calibration constant

The paper's constant, as the dongle holds it. It is the "known lux × known time" product of the paper calibration, not a value you type here.

Measure

One tap starts a SENSOR read, stores it as the exposure reading, and asks the dongle to compute. While the dongle is working, the last answer stays on screen and the button is disabled.

Filter Grade Transform

The grade rail shows the grade tokens the dongle's table holds for the selected paper and filter brand. A grade is a request, not a local choice: the app sends FILTER brand= grade= and the meter answers. The line below the rail explains the current state:

  • No filter grade — the time is the unfiltered one;
  • No filtration — the time is the unfiltered one;
  • Grade 2xM1 — the factor is the meter's.

If there is no table for the paper and brand, the card says No grade table for this paper and filter brand instead of drawing an empty rail.

Dodge & Burn

A symmetric slider: the lit span runs from the centre to the thumb, and the default middle position has no fill. The value is in quarter stops. This is the one trim on Exposure; the four trims live on Contrast and Split.

3.3 Step by step

  1. Confirm the top bar says Ready.
  2. Choose the paper and filter brand from the selection bar.
  3. Swipe the zone rail to the zone you are metering; V is the usual start.
  4. Put the sensor on the easel and tap Measure.
  5. Read the time. Set the enlarger and the filter grade; the grade is the suggested one in the answer line.
  6. If the print needs a little more or less, use Dodge & Burn and measure again, or adjust the trim on Contrast.

3.4 The zone list

The rail runs 0 to X because those are the meter's own numbers.

ZoneWhat it represents
0The black end: deep shadow with texture
I–IIIThe low values
IVA darker midtone
VMiddle grey: the standard metering target
VIA lighter midtone
VII–IXThe high values
XThe white end: a specular or paper-base highlight

Meter the tone you want to print as middle grey. If you meter a highlight, the time will make that highlight middle grey, which is usually not what you want.

3.5 What the filter grade does

A variable-contrast filter changes the paper's speed as well as its contrast. The dongle knows the factor for each grade in its table, so the time already includes the filter. You do not multiply by a filter factor yourself.

The grade is independent of the zone. The zone chooses which tone becomes middle grey; the grade chooses the contrast. Changing one does not silently change the other.

3.6 Dodge and burn

The burn slider is a bias: it shifts the whole exposure, not a local dodge. It is measured in quarter stops and is symmetric around zero. Use it when the print is consistently a little light or dark but the contrast is right.

The four trims on Contrast and Split are the per-print adjustments: exposure, contrast, highlights and shadows. They are saved per paper and per tool.

3.7 A worked example

Suppose the meter says 12.40 s, grade 2xM1, zone V. Set the enlarger to 12.4 seconds and the filter to the 2xM1 grade. Make the print.

If the print is slightly light across the whole image, open Dodge & Burn and move one step toward + (a quarter stop). If the contrast is right but the highlights are blocked, use the Highlights trim on Contrast instead. The trim is the more surgical control; the burn is the global one.

3.8 Common questions

The time is blank. The dongle has not answered a compute yet. Measure, or check that the paper has a calibration.

The time says calibrate. The paper has no calibration constant. Calibrate the paper (chapter 10).

The grade rail is missing. The paper and brand have no grade table; the card says so. Try another brand, or edit the paper in the Paper & Filter Editor.

The app says No meter. Check the cable and the Android USB permission; open Setup → Meter → Reconnect.

4. Contrast

4.1 What the two readings mean

Contrast uses two readings:

  • the highlight: the dim spot under the enlarger, where you want detail in the print;
  • the shadow: the bright spot, where you want the dark areas to separate.

The dongle compares them and answers with a time and a suggested grade. The two readings are stored on the dongle; changing paper or grade asks the dongle to re-price the same two readings, so you do not have to go back to the easel.

4.2 The screen

  • Time and Grade share the answer well. Both values use the same font size; if one has to shrink to fit, the other shrinks with it.
  • Highlights and Shadows are capture tiles. Each shows the physical hint, the lux and its Measure action.
  • Fine tune holds the four trims and the burn. It is collapsed until you open it.
  • Dodge & Burn is the same symmetric burn slider as Exposure.

The line under the two values carries the midpoint lux, the range, the grade label, the match and the burn. It is limited to two lines; if it would need a third, it shrinks just enough instead of pushing the rest of the screen down.

4.3 Step by step

  1. Confirm the paper and filter brand.
  2. Tap Measure on Highlights and meter the dim spot.
  3. Tap Measure on Shadows and meter the bright spot.
  4. Read Time and Grade in the answer well.
  5. Open Fine tune if the print needs adjustment; use the trims for highlights, shadows, exposure and contrast, and the burn for a global shift.
  6. Reset puts every trim and the burn back to neutral. It does not clear the two readings.

4.4 How the recommendation works, without the maths

The dongle turns the two lux values into a density range, compares that range with the paper's response and chooses the grade whose contrast fits. The time is the exposure that places the highlight and shadow where the paper can hold them. You do not need the formula; you need the two readings and a calibrated paper.

4.5 Fixed-grade papers

A fixed-grade paper has no variable-contrast ladder. The grade rail shows the paper's fixed grade, and Contrast still gives a time from the two readings. Changing to another grade is not offered because the paper cannot use one.

4.6 A worked example

Meter the brightest area you want to keep detail in as Highlights; meter the darkest area you want to keep separation in as Shadows. The answer might be 8.4 s at grade 2xM1. Set the enlarger to 8.4 seconds and the filter to 2xM1.

If the print is too contrasty, move the Contrast trim toward − in Fine tune. If the highlights are too bright, move Highlights toward −. The trims are per paper and per tool, so they survive a session change.

4.7 Common questions

The answer says No time. At least one spot has no reading. The hints under the tiles tell you which one is missing.

The time did not change when I changed the paper. The app re-asks the dongle when the paper change is confirmed; if the dongle is not ready, the old answer stays. Check the top bar and Setup → Meter.

The values have different sizes. They should not: the two columns share one fitted size. If you see a difference, the app is not the current build.

5. Split Grade

5.1 The idea

A split-grade print uses two exposures through two filters: a soft leg for the highlights and a hard leg for the shadows. The dongle measures the same two spots as Contrast and answers with a soft time and a hard time.

5.2 The screen

The answer well shows Soft and Hard side by side. The two values share a font size, so the pair stays symmetrical. Under them are the conditions and the midpoint.

The two capture tiles are the same highlight/shadow pair as Contrast. Fine tune adds one control that Contrast does not have: the Midtones pair. The pair is the meter's own soft/hard ladder position; Reset resets it to the ladder's centre together with the four trims.

5.3 Step by step

  1. Choose the paper and brand.
  2. Meter the dim spot as Highlights.
  3. Meter the bright spot as Shadows.
  4. Read Soft and Hard.
  5. Expose the print in two steps: the soft time through the soft filter, then the hard time through the hard filter. Cover the paper between the two.
  6. If the print needs a different split, adjust Midtones in Fine tune; the dongle recalculates the pair from the stored readings.

5.4 How the split is chosen, without the maths

The dongle divides the tonal range between the two filters. The soft leg holds the highlight and the hard leg builds the shadow. The Midtones control moves the balance between the legs; it is not an exposure compensation and not a contrast trim.

5.5 A worked example

The answer might be Soft 5.2 s and Hard 3.1 s at grade 2. Expose 5.2 seconds through the soft filter, then 3.1 seconds through the hard filter. If the midtones are too heavy, move Midtones toward the hard side and make another print; the dongle keeps the same two readings.

5.6 Common questions

One time is missing. The pair is computed only when both spots exist. The hint under the missing tile says which spot to meter.

Reset did not change the times. Reset clears the trims and the Midtones pair; the times are recomputed from the same two readings. If the paper has no pair table, the Midtones row is inert.

The two times look different in size. They share one fitted size by design. If they do not, update the app.

6. Virtual Proof

6.1 What it does

Virtual Proof turns a grid of easel readings into a picture of the print. In normal (negative) mode, the cells show the meter's grayscale proof: where the print will be light, where it will be dark, and which cells are clipped.

In Enlarger Mode, the same grid measures the enlarger's evenness: the cells show deviation from the reference, and the answer is a uniformity verdict.

6.2 The screen

  • The cell canvas is the main surface. The controls that move it are at the bottom of the same card: Start scan, Set V Zone (or Set Reference in Enlarger Mode), Clear Grid, the status line, and the Columns / Rows steppers.
  • Selected sample shows the tapped cell's readouts.
  • Result shows the measured count, range, mean, min, max and range fit. In normal mode it does not show Uniformity, Min/max spread or Worst cell; those belong to Enlarger Mode.
  • Filter grade shows the proof grade rail. It is the grid's own grade, not the Exposure grade.
  • Histogram is a disclosure card.
  • Settings is a disclosure card below the histogram.

The explaining legend below the canvas is not permanent. It appears as a dismissible banner only after a completed scan.

6.3 The grid frames

  • Red frame: the selected cell; its values are in Selected sample.
  • Muted red / orange frame: the next cell the scan will write.
  • Dark red frame: the Zone V reference cell.
  • Bright or dim edge: the cell is clipped at the highlight or shadow end.
  • Gray fill: the meter's proof tone, 0 black to 255 white.

The legend is a reminder, not a second control list. The same information is in this chapter.

6.4 A proof in ten steps

  1. Choose the paper and filter brand.
  2. Open Proof.
  3. Set Columns and Rows; 3 × 3 is a good first proof.
  4. Tap Start scan. The dongle measures each cell in turn.
  5. If you scan by hand, move the sensor to the next cell and tap the action again. The app names the next cell.
  6. Let the scan complete. The legend banner appears; read it once, then close it if you do not need it.
  7. Tap a cell to inspect its Selected sample.
  8. Read Result for the measured count and range.
  9. Use Histogram if you want the distribution; it is above Settings.
  10. Use Settings for Stability Detection, tolerance and the settle gate.

Stop appears while a scan is running. Clear Grid starts a new proof; it does not change the paper or the calibration.

Note

Set V Zone takes the selected measured cell as the grid's reference. In Enlarger Mode the same button is called Set Reference. It is enabled only when the tapped cell can serve as the anchor.

6.5 Enlarger Mode

Turn on Enlarger Mode in the Settings card. The answer well appears at the top with the uniformity verdict; the result rows include Uniformity and Worst cell. Use the grid to find hot spots and falloff in the enlarger's light.

When Enlarger Mode is off, the verdict is not shown; the canvas is the main theme and the result stays a print result. This is deliberate: a uniformity percentage is meaningless for a negative proof.

7. Setup

7.1 The index

Tap Setup. The index groups the pages by what they belong to:

GroupRowWhat it opens
DeviceMeterConnection, firmware, serial and board
DevicePaper & filterThe same sheet as the selection bar
CalibrationCalibrationThe paper's known lux and known time
CalibrationSensorGain, integration time, averaging and Sensor Calibration
WorkTools & dataPaper editor, estimate and files
WorkHelp & messagesWhat a refusal means and where to fix it
WorkAboutVersion and the data rule

7.2 Meter

The Meter page reports what the dongle said when it connected: the firmware version, the protocol, the board and the serial number. The SafelightIO ID is shown as SN: ..., the chip's uppercase unique board ID, just as the 7-inch device shows it. Use it to tell two dongles apart. Reconnect asks the app to open the port and send HELLO again.

Use it when the top bar is stuck on No meter or Linking, or after a firmware update. If the dongle is not attached, the page says so; it cannot invent a connection.

7.3 Calibration

The Calibration page is the paper's two numbers:

  • Known lux: the light measured on the test strip;
  • Known time (s): the exposure that produced the chosen midtone.

The page shows the paper the dongle has in force, whether it has a calibration, the meter's constant and the phone's copy when one exists. Enter the pair and send it; the dongle stores it for that paper.

For a fixed-grade paper, the page still takes the pair; there is no grade ladder to choose. Use the same midtone procedure.

7.4 Sensor

The Sensor page has three controls:

  • Gain — a snap rail: Auto, Low, Med, High, Max.
  • Integration time (ms) — a snap rail from 100 to 600 ms.
  • Averaging samples — a number field, 1–16.

The page also shows:

  • Effective gain — the rung the meter resolved, or the manual gain it is using;
  • A read may take — the time budget for one reading;
  • the provenance line — whether the settings came from the meter or the phone;
  • the phone's backup copy, when one exists.

Auto is the normal choice; a manual rung is for a difficult subject or for checking the sensor's behaviour.

Sensor Calibration

At the bottom of the Sensor page is the Sensor Calibration card. It holds Calibrate Dark and Calibrate Enlarger Light, plus Clear Dark and Clear Light. Do the dark calibration with the sensor covered and the light calibration with the enlarger on. This is the one-time job that makes the lux numbers trustworthy.

Important

A paper calibration on top of an uncalibrated sensor gives a time, but the lux numbers under it are not trustworthy. The sensor calibration is the foundation for the paper calibration, not an optional extra.

8. Tools & data

Open Setup → Work → Tools & data. It has three cards.

8.1 Paper & Filter Editor

The editor changes the paper's coefficients on the dongle. Choose the filter and the paper; the editor shows the Lengthening Factor, the ISO R Range and the Base ISO P. For a fixed-grade paper, the factor and ISO R fields are inert and the fixed grade is shown instead; the Base ISO P is editable.

The editor is an advanced tool. If you only need to choose a paper that is already in the catalogue, use Paper & filter instead.

8.2 Estimate Calibration

The estimate card gives a starting calibration when you do not have a test strip. It uses the paper's ISO P and the reference paper to estimate the pair. Treat the result as a starting point and confirm it with a real strip.

8.3 Data Manager

The Data Manager saves and loads two kinds of file on the phone:

  • Settings: the dongle's persistent settings, including the paper catalogue and calibrations;
  • Session: the current tool's readings, trims and selections.

A load always shows a preview and asks for confirmation before it writes anything to the dongle. Save writes a text file to the phone; Load opens one after the preview. The app never silently restores a file at launch.

9. Saving, loading and storage

9.1 What is saved automatically

The dongle persists the paper, the filter brand and grade, the paper calibrations, the sensor settings, the trims and the burn. The app reads them on every connection. You do not need to press Save to keep the ordinary working state.

The app's own view is not a file. Switching tools, rotating the phone or reopening the app does not lose the dongle's settings because they are on the dongle.

9.2 Settings files

A Settings file is a backup of the dongle's persistent state. Use it when you want a copy on the phone, or when you are moving to another dongle. The file is a text document; the Data Manager preview shows what it contains before you load it.

9.3 Session files

A Session file stores the current tool's readings, trims and selections. It is useful when you want to come back to a print after a break, or when you want to keep the two readings from a Contrast or Split session.

Loading a session restores the readings and the trims; it does not change the paper calibration or the paper catalogue unless the file contains those groups. The preview always says what will be written.

9.4 What is kept, and what is not

DataLives on
Paper catalogueDongle
Paper calibrationDongle (and in a Settings file when saved)
Filter brand and gradeDongle
Sensor gain, integration, averagingDongle
Trims and burnDongle, per paper and per tool
Current readingsApp session; not on the dongle after a power cycle
Settings and Session filesPhone documents, only when you save them
App version and codePhone

The dongle does not persist the current readings. If you unplug it, the readings leave with the app's session; save a Session file if you need them later.

10. Calibrating a paper

10.1 Before you start

You need:

  • a calibrated sensor (chapter 7.4);
  • the paper and the filter brand you will print with;
  • a test strip and the reference print you are matching;
  • a way to measure the light on the strip.

The paper calibration is one-time per paper and filter. Redo it when you change developer, toner, or the paper's response.

10.2 Procedure

  1. Make a test strip with a series of exposures, usually in half or third stops.
  2. Develop it exactly as you will develop the print.
  3. Choose the patch that matches the reference midtone. This is the known time: the exposure that produced that patch.
  4. Measure the light on that patch with the meter. This is the known lux.
  5. Open Setup → Calibration (or Tools & data → Estimate Calibration).
  6. Enter Known lux and Known time (s); send the pair.
  7. The dongle multiplies the known lux by the known time to get the paper's constant. The app confirms the constant it read back.
  8. Make a print at the meter's suggested time. The print should match the reference midtone; if it does not, check the sensor calibration before repeating the strip.

10.3 What "correct midtone" means

The correct patch is the one that matches the tone you want middle grey to be, not the one that looks "nice" in isolation. Use the same reference print and the same viewing light each time. A darkroom's safelight can make a print look darker than it is; judge under the enlarger's white light or a consistent viewing light.

10.4 Redoing a calibration

Redo the paper calibration when:

  • you change developer or dilution;
  • you change the paper's grade or the paper itself;
  • the prints are consistently off in the same direction;
  • you have replaced the sensor or the dongle.

You do not need to redo it for every print, every session, or every filter change. The filter factor is part of the dongle's table, not the paper calibration.

10.5 Fixed-grade papers

A fixed-grade paper has no variable-contrast ladder. The calibration pair is still lux and time; the grade is fixed by the paper. The editor and the calibration page show the fixed grade and make the factor/ISO R fields inert.

10.6 A calibration checklist

  • Sensor dark calibration done.
  • Sensor light calibration done with the enlarger at the working height.
  • Paper and filter brand selected.
  • Test strip developed exactly like the print.
  • Midtone chosen under consistent light.
  • Known lux and known time entered for the right paper.
  • The dongle answered with a constant; the app shows it.
  • A confirm print matches the reference.

10.7 Worked examples

Example 1 — the first calibration

You expose a strip in one-stop steps and the 8-second patch matches your reference midtone. You measure 1.20 lux on that patch. Enter 1.20 lux and 8 seconds. The dongle stores the product; the Exposure answer for a 0.30 lux reading is then about 32 seconds.

Example 2 — a developer change

You change from a paper developer to a warmer, slower developer. The prints are consistently light. Make a new strip with the new developer, choose the new midtone patch, and enter the new pair. Do not compensate with the burn; the burn is for a print that is consistently off for a different reason.

Example 3 — a fixed-grade paper

The fixed-grade paper's calibration page still asks for known lux and known time. Choose the patch that matches the reference; the fixed grade is already part of the paper's response.

Example 4 — no strip looks right

If no patch matches, check the sensor calibration first, then the developer temperature and the paper's age. A paper calibration cannot repair a sensor that is reading the wrong lux.

Example 5 — a second paper from a reference

If you have a calibrated paper and want a starting point for another, use Estimate Calibration, then make a strip to confirm. An estimate is a starting point, not a calibration.

11. The paper and filter database

11.1 Where the catalogue lives

The paper catalogue is on the dongle. The app does not ship a copy. On every connection the app reads the dongle's PAPERS block: the paper brands, the paper types and the filter brands. That is why the sheet says Connect the meter to list papers when no dongle is attached.

The catalogue includes the paper's filter system, its kind (variable or fixed grade) and its filter table. The app uses those fields to decide which grades are offered and whether the Midtones pair is available.

11.2 Filter brands

The Filter brand rail lists the brands the dongle knows. A brand is half of the selection: FILTER brand= grade=. The brand is shown in the selection bar; the grade is chosen on Exposure.

11.3 Adding your own paper

Open Setup → Tools & data → Paper & Filter Editor. Choose the paper and the filter, then edit the coefficients:

  • Lengthening Factor: the paper's speed factor;
  • ISO R Range: the contrast range;
  • Base ISO P: the paper's ISO speed.

For a fixed-grade paper, the factor and ISO R fields are inert; the Base ISO P is editable. Reset restores the paper's defaults after a confirmation.

Note

The editor writes to the dongle. Another phone will see the edited paper only after it reads the dongle's catalogue again. There is no cloud copy and no bundled fallback.

12. Filter factors

12.1 What a filter factor is

A filter factor is a multiplier on the exposure: a factor of 2 means one stop more light. Variable-contrast filters have different factors at different grades, which is why the grade and the time are linked in the dongle's table.

12.2 Measuring your own factor, simply

  1. Meter a plain, even grey target without the filter and note the time.
  2. Meter the same target with the filter and note the time.
  3. Divide the filtered time by the unfiltered time. The result is the factor.

Do this at the grade you actually use. The filter's factor is not a constant across all grades.

12.3 Re-measuring

Re-measure the factor when you change the filter brand, the paper, or the light source. The dongle's table is the starting point; your own measurement is the confirmation.

12.4 Long exposures

Very long exposures can lose contrast through reciprocity. The meter does not invent a reciprocity correction; if your paper's data sheet gives one, apply it as a deliberate exposure adjustment and note it in the session, not as a paper calibration.

13. Messages and troubleshooting

13.1 The top bar

What you seeWhat it meansWhat to do

LinkingThe port is open; the app is waiting for HELLOWait a moment; then Setup → Meter → Reconnect

No reply / a short errorThe port opened but the dongle did not answerUnplug, replug, reconnect
Firmware too oldThe dongle cannot list papersUpdate the firmware (chapter 14)

13.2 The common refusals

The app quotes the dongle's own sentence. The words are the firmware's, not a summary.

SentenceMeaningRoute
select paperNo paper is in forceTap the selection bar and choose a paper
calibrateThe paper has no calibrationCalibrate the paper (chapter 10)
no paperThe dongle has no paper selectedChoose a paper
no_dataThe paper and brand have no table row for that gradeChoose another grade or brand
bad_argA token the firmware does not acceptCheck the value; use the in-app control

select a measured cellSet V Zone has no valid selected cellTap a measured cell

The Help & messages page in the app explains the current sentence and the route to the fix.

13.3 Troubleshooting

The app never leaves No meter

  • Use a data cable, not a charge-only cable.
  • Accept the Android USB permission.
  • Close any other app that holds the USB port.
  • Try another USB-C port or OTG adapter.
  • Open Setup → Meter → Reconnect.

The top bar says Ready but there is no paper

  • The dongle may have no paper selected; open Paper & filter.
  • The catalogue read may still be in flight; wait a moment.
  • Use Setup → Meter to see the firmware and the catalogue state.

The times are consistently wrong

  • Check the sensor calibration: dark and enlarger light.
  • Check the paper calibration pair.
  • Check that the paper in force is the paper on the easel.
  • Check the filter brand and grade; a wrong brand gives a wrong factor.

Contrast or Split says one spot is missing

  • The hint under the tile names the missing spot.
  • Meter it; the answer appears when both readings exist.
  • A 0.00 lux reading is a real reading, not a missing one.

The proof grid is empty

  • The paper must be selected and the dongle ready.
  • Start scan or measure the next cell; the canvas fills as readings arrive.
  • If the scan stops early, the remaining cells stay empty; that is a valid partial proof.

A firmware update fails

  • Do not unplug until the RP2350 drive disappears.
  • If the update is interrupted, try the 1200-baud touch again.
  • If the app no longer starts and the touch does not work, the unit needs a service recovery; a sealed unit has no BOOTSEL button. See chapter 14.

14. Firmware updates

14.1 Check your version

The top bar shows Ready · fw 0.11 (or your version). Setup → Meter shows the firmware, protocol, board and serial number. Write the version down before an update.

14.2 Update with the 1200-baud touch

The dongle has no BOOTSEL button. Its USB serial stack supports the standard Pico 1200-baud touch: opening the port at 1200 baud asks the running firmware to reset into the RP2350 ROM bootloader. The ROM exposes the RP2350 USB drive.

  1. Save any Session file you need. The update does not change the paper catalogue or the calibrations, but a backup is cheap.
  2. Plug the dongle into the computer with a data cable.
  3. Open the dongle's serial port at 1200 baud and close it.
  • macOS: screen /dev/cu.usbmodem* 1200, then quit.
  • Windows: a terminal program with the COM port set to 1200.
  • Linux: stty -F /dev/ttyACM0 1200, then close.
  1. Wait for the RP2350 drive to appear.
  2. Copy the new .uf2 onto that drive.
  3. Wait until the drive disappears. Do not unplug during the copy.
  4. Reconnect the dongle to the phone; the top bar should return to Ready with the new version.

No SDK or Picotool is required on the computer. The 1200-baud touch is a feature of the firmware's USB serial stack, not a separate program.

Warning

The 1200-baud touch only works while the current firmware runs. If an update is interrupted, the app may no longer start and the touch may not respond. The unit then needs a service recovery. Keep the cable connected until the RP2350 drive disappears, and do not update on a low phone battery or a flaky hub.

14.3 What is kept

The firmware update replaces the program, not the paper catalogue or the calibrations. The dongle's persistent records are kept. The phone's Settings and Session files are not touched.

If the update includes a storage-format change, the release notes will say so; read them before updating.

14.4 If the update does not start

  • Check the cable is a data cable.
  • Close the app on the phone; the phone and the computer cannot both own the port.
  • Try another serial terminal; the port name changes each time the dongle reconnects.
  • If the port opens but no RP2350 appears, the firmware may not be running; see the warning above.

15.2 Glossary

Calibration constant — the paper's lux × time product; the number the meter divides by the light reading.

Contrast — the tool that reads a highlight and a shadow and returns a time and a grade.

Dongle — the USB meter: sensor, RP2350, catalogue and records. It has no screen.

Exposure — the one-spot tool: choose a zone, measure, get a time.

Filter brand — the manufacturer of the variable-contrast filter; the brand selects the grade table.

Filter grade — the contrast grade, such as 2xM1; chosen on Exposure, stored on the dongle.

Fine tune — the collapsed Contrast/Split card holding the four trims and the burn.

Paper calibration — the one-time test-strip pair that gives the paper its constant.

Proof — the grid tool that previews the print, or in Enlarger Mode checks the light's evenness.

Split — the two-filter tool: a soft time and a hard time from the same two spots.

Trim — a per-paper, per-tool adjustment to exposure, contrast, highlights or shadows.

15.4 One-page cheat sheet

  1. Connect: dongle → phone; allow USB; wait for Ready.
  2. Choose: selection bar → Filter brand, then paper.
  3. Exposure: zone rail → V; Measure; use the time and grade.
  4. Contrast: meter Highlights, then Shadows; use Time and Grade.
  5. Split: the same two spots; use Soft and Hard; Midtones in Fine tune.
  6. Proof: set the grid; Start scan; tap a cell; read Result.
  7. Calibrate: sensor first, then paper; one test strip sets the constant.
  8. Update: open the serial port at 1200; copy the UF2 to RP2350; wait.

Tip

The app's Help & messages page quotes the dongle's own refusal and the route to the fix. The Setup → Meter page is the first place to look when the connection is not Ready.
